transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-07
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Harper (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Tom Reyes (Redwood Product), Maya Patel (LighthouseHealth ML Eng), Jon Ruiz (CTO), Sara Kim (Product Lead), Speaker 1 (Legal?)
Recording note: participant audio levels vary; occasional background noise and overlapping talk

Summary:
Quick walkthrough of Redwood's model catalog, benching approach, compatibility matrix and a proposed bench/run plan for LighthouseHealth's clinical summarization flows. Discussed hosted vs private, routing fallbacks, latency/cost tradeoffs and compliance considerations (KMS, audit logs). Agreed next steps to run an initial benchmark and share artifacts.

Topics covered:
- Catalog UI: filters, compatibility flags, kernel mapping
- Bench methodology: p99 latency, throughput, quality evals, cost-per-1000 tokens
- Routing & fallback: variant selection by latency/cost
- Private deployment constraints: VPC, KMS, SOC2 questions
- Pilot scope and timeline

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Alex Harper: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Alex from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. We'll do a quick catalog walkthrough and then Priya will go into the bench plan and the runtime compatibility bits.
[00:00:12] Jon Ruiz: Great, thanks. We've got about an hour, so let's focus on the parts that matter for performance and compliance.
[00:00:18] Maya Patel: Yes, and I put our key success criteria in the calendar note — p99 under 700ms on common prompts and cost under our current baseline which is roughly $0.12 per 1k tokens right now.
[00:00:28] Priya Singh: Cool, Maya. Quick note: our catalog pages show model family, estimated latency per hardware profile, and a compatibility matrix to show kernel/quantization fit. Those numbers are measured with Redwood's continuous runner and are a heuristic, you'll want to run your prompt set to get final numbers.
[00:00:43] Sara Kim: When you say compatibility matrix, is that about what GPUs a model can run on, or also about things like quantization accuracy and structured output?
[00:00:52] Priya Singh: Both. It flags hardware compatibility (A100, H100, T4), kernel maturity (optimized kernels available), quantization-friendly label, and special notes for structured-output models. We also annotate fallbacks — like if the primary variant uses fp16 on H100 but the fallback on T4 will use 4-bit quantized and may have a latency/cost tradeoff.
[00:01:12] Jon Ruiz: Okay — our main concern is quality regression when we go to quantized variants. How do you capture quality deltas in the catalog?
[00:01:20] Tom Reyes: We store eval signals tied to prompt sets and have a delta indicator — red/amber/green — that shows expected degradation against a baseline. For LighthouseHealth we'd run your sample prompts and get a per-model delta and actual generated examples in the bench report.
[00:01:35] Speaker 1: Can I interrupt for a compliance question? Do you store the prompts or outputs anywhere in hosted mode?
[00:01:41] Alex Harper: Short answer: hosted mode stores minimal metadata for observability but you can opt out of retention; private and dedicated can be set to not retain payloads, and we integrate with KMS for key management. We'll share the SOC2 and data retention docs after.
[00:01:55] Maya Patel: That's important — we have PHI concerns, so we'll probably prefer a private deployment or at least strict retention controls.
[00:02:02] Priya Singh: Understood. For the bench, we can run the initial bucket in our dedicated infra with no payload retention. Or we can coordinate the benchmark runner to execute in your VPC if you prefer on-prem-like isolation.
[00:02:15] Jon Ruiz: How long does a typical catalog-driven bench take? If we give you 50 prompts, what do you need?
[00:02:22] Priya Singh: For 50 prompts at multiple seq lengths and a few temperature/beam settings, a 2-hour run typically yields stable latency/throughput estimates plus sample outputs for quality checks. We'll also collect cost-per-1k estimate.
[00:02:33] Sara Kim: What's the delta between the catalog's estimated latency and what you typically see in an org's own prompts?
[00:02:40] Priya Singh: Usually within 10–25% depending on prompt shape and KV cache behavior. If you have long context reuse patterns, the runtime benefits from KV caching and you'll see better per-token latency after warm-up.
[00:02:52] Maya Patel: We have a lot of prefix reuse — templates with dynamic fields — so KV caching could help. How does Redwood surface caching benefits?
[00:02:59] Tom Reyes: We include cache-hit assumptions in the bench report and show both cold p95/p99 and warmed p95/p99. That usually helps decide routing policies — e.g., route high-change single-turn queries to lower-cost variants, keep chat-like flows on higher-throughput pools.
[00:03:15] Alex Harper: Quick demo now — I'll share my screen and walk through the catalog. (screen switches)
[00:03:25] [00:03:25] Alex Harper: On the left you can filter by task (summarization, chat, code), then by latency tiers and hardware. I'm selecting summarization and toggling to show only open models that have 4-bit quant support flagged.
[00:03:40] Maya Patel: I see a note that model "odysseus-13b-quant" has a green quality delta for short-form medical summary but amber for long-form. Is that empirical?
[00:03:49] Priya Singh: That's from our small-scale eval. We run prompt families and compute ROUGE-type heuristics plus human checks for sensitive domains. For long-form we sometimes prefer a higher-precision variant.
[00:03:59] Jon Ruiz: How do we pin models in production and enforce rollbacks if quality drops?
[00:04:06] Alex Harper: In the Console you can pin a model version for a given route. We also support canary rollouts and automatic fallback — if p95 latency exceeds threshold or error rates spike, traffic shifts to the pinned fallback variant.
[00:04:17] Sara Kim: Can the fallback be a different model family entirely? Like fall back from a 4-bit opt model to a smaller full-precision model?
[00:04:24] Priya Singh: Yes — we let you configure compatible fallbacks; the routing layer will only pick variants that we've declared compatible for your route. You can also define cost budgets per route.
[00:04:34] [00:04:34] Maya Patel: What's the cost reporting cadence? We need token-level visibility for chargeback to product teams.
[00:04:40] Tom Reyes: We provide per-token cost breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and per-token attribution in the Console. You can export CSVs and integrate with your billing systems.
[00:04:49] Jon Ruiz: Let's talk about the bench plan then — what do you need from us?
[00:04:53] Priya Singh: Three things: 1) a representative prompt set (we asked for ~50 to start), 2) target SLOs (latency/cost/quality), and 3) a preferred deployment for the run (hosted dedicated test infra or runner in your VPC).
[00:05:04] Maya Patel: We'll provide prompts and SLOs. For deployment, we want to test both hosted-dedicated and an emulated private run to understand differences.
[00:05:12] Priya Singh: Perfect. For the hosted-dedicated run we can run on our Dedicated GPU pool; for the private-run emulation we can run the same runner but with network restrictions and no retention, or we can run the runner in your VPC.
[00:05:24] Speaker 1: Any compliance risks with the runner in our VPC?
[00:05:28] Alex Harper: If the runner runs in your VPC under your account, there's no payload retention on our side. We'll still need network and auth setup; we can share a checklist.
[00:05:36] Sara Kim: How do you handle keys? We use AWS KMS and HSM for certain keys.
[00:05:40] Tom Reyes: We integrate with KMS and can accept wrapped keys or use customer-managed keys in Private deployments. We'll attach the security architecture note to the spreadsheet.
[00:05:48] [00:05:48] Priya Singh: Back to the catalog: there's also a compatibility column for runtime kernels. For example, some Llama-variant forks have a mature fused attention kernel and show a 20–40% latency win on H100. That gets surfaced as a kernel maturity score.
[00:06:04] Maya Patel: Are those kernel maturity scores validated for long contexts? Because our summaries sometimes include 8k context windows.
[00:06:10] Priya Singh: We run scaled tests up to 16k for select models; the maturity score includes long-context metrics when available. For models without long-context kernels we flag them.
[00:06:20] Jon Ruiz: We have a hard requirement to keep p99 under 1.2s for the interactive clinician workflow. Can you show us which open models in the catalog are likely candidates?
[00:06:29] Alex Harper: Sure — filtering by p99 < 1.2s on H100 and green quality for medical summarization gives a shortlist: odysseus-13b, aurora-14b-opt, and luma-7b-advanced. Each has tradeoffs on cost and quantization.
[00:06:43] Sara Kim: Luma-7b looks promising cost-wise but is the quality adequate for clinical tone?
[00:06:49] Priya Singh: For short templated clinical notes it's often fine; for tone and detail we tend to see the 13–14b families score higher. We'll include sample outputs per prompt in the bench report so you can audit tone.
[00:07:02] [00:07:02] Maya Patel: About routing — can we route based on user tier? e.g. clinicians go to higher-precision family, admin portal uses cheaper variants?
[00:07:09] Tom Reyes: Yes, route by token budget, route by user attribute, or even by region. The Console supports route rules and priorities.
[00:07:16] Jon Ruiz: For the pilot, I want cost projections. How precise are your cost estimates?
[00:07:21] Alex Harper: Catalog estimates assume average token lengths and standard batch sizes; bench runs output observed cost-per-1k tokens for your actual prompts which is more accurate. Usually estimates are within 15–30% until we run your exact workload.
[00:07:34] [00:07:34] Sara Kim: Can we get automated alerts if quality regresses after a rollout?
[00:07:38] Priya Singh: Yes — Optimize ties to eval suites. You can pin an eval set; if distributional metrics change beyond thresholds we send quality regression alerts and can auto-roll back traffic.
[00:07:49] Maya Patel: Great. We also need audit logs for all inference calls for compliance.
[00:07:54] Tom Reyes: We have request-level audit logs, and for Private we can keep full payload logs if you want; for hosted we keep metadata unless you opt into retention.
[00:08:03] [00:08:03] Speaker 1: Will you share the SOC2 and encryption docs? We need them ahead of legal review.
[00:08:07] Alex Harper: Yes, I'll attach the SOC2 report, encryption whitepaper, and the network checklist in a follow-up email.
[00:08:15] Jon Ruiz: Okay next, an example bench run — Priya?
[00:08:18] Priya Singh: I'll walk through the bench spreadsheet. (shared) First column is prompt id, second is prompt shape, then we list median token length, sample outputs, cold p95/p99, warmed p95/p99, tokens-per-second, and estimated cost per 1k tokens. We also have a quality score where we mark pass/fail against your rubric.
[00:08:38] Maya Patel: What's the quality rubric look like?
[00:08:41] Priya Singh: We'll co-design it with you, but typical axes are factuality, completeness, PHI stripping where required, and tone. We can add a custom rule for medical tone.
[00:08:52] Sara Kim: Can we add human-in-the-loop checks for the first few thousand outputs?
[00:08:56] Priya Singh: Absolutely. Optimize supports sampling outputs to a review queue and can bind human labels back into the eval set.
[00:09:04] [00:09:04] Alex Harper: Quick pause for clarifying question from Jon.
[00:09:07] Jon Ruiz: One of our big concerns is spiky traffic during morning rounds — does Redwood autoscale fast enough to keep latency SLOs?
[00:09:16] Priya Singh: Our Dedicated pools have autoscaling with burst capacity; autoscale is tuned to keep p95/p99 targets. For very sudden spikes, routing policies can backfill to another region or fallback variant to keep errors low. We can show historical scaling graphs in Console.
[00:09:30] Maya Patel: What are realistic warm-up times for the KV cache? We often have many small conversations.
[00:09:36] Tom Reyes: With continuous reuse patterns, warm-up can be a few requests for hot prefixes; for very rare prefixes it won't help much. We show warmed vs cold lines so you can pick routes that benefit.
[00:09:48] [00:09:48] Speaker 1: Legal follow-up — do you support data processing addendum (DPA) and BAA for health customers?
[00:09:55] Alex Harper: We support DPA; for BAAs we'll escalate to our legal team — we've signed BAAs with health customers before. I'll mark that as an action item.
[00:10:03] Jon Ruiz: Good. Let's make this concrete: can you run a two-phase pilot? Phase 1: bench with our 50 prompts in your dedicated infra and sample private-run emulation. Phase 2: a 4-week pilot on a small set of routes with monitoring and alerts.
[00:10:15] Priya Singh: Yep that aligns to our usual path. Phase 1 will give us baseline numbers and Phase 2 will stress test with real traffic and monitoring hooks.
[00:10:23] Sara Kim: Timeline?
[00:10:25] Alex Harper: If you send prompts by 2026-10-11 we can run bench by 2026-10-13 and deliver report by 2026-10-15. Pilot could start late October pending legal and infra setup.
[00:10:35] Maya Patel: That works on our side.
[00:10:38] [00:10:38] Priya Singh: I'll quickly demo how to schedule a bench in Console. (screen) There's a "Bench Run" button off the model detail page, choose your prompt set (we can upload on your behalf or you can), select hardware and run options: cold vs warmed, retention on/off, and we include sample output inspection.
[00:10:58] Maya Patel: Can we test with different temperature and beam settings automatically?
[00:11:02] Priya Singh: Yes, parameter sweeps are supported. We'll show matrix results in the report.
[00:11:08] Jon Ruiz: Any gotchas we should know before handing over prompts?
[00:11:12] Alex Harper: Avoid disclosing real patient identifiers in the sample prompts if you don't want them retained; masked prompts are fine. Also include expected context lengths and representative token sizes.
[00:11:23] Sara Kim: Will you add cost estimates for the private emulation run?
[00:11:26] Tom Reyes: We'll show comparative cost: hosted-dedicated vs private-emulation (which approximates infra costs). We'll note where private infra has different kernel availability which can change latency.
[00:11:36] [00:11:36] Maya Patel: One more question on model pinning: if we pin a version and later a security patch appears for the runtime, can you force-upgrade?
[00:11:43] Priya Singh: We notify customers of critical security updates; for managed deployments we can schedule upgrades during maintenance windows. If you pin a model version the control plane still applies security patches to the runtime unless you have an isolated on-prem deployment.
[00:11:58] Alex Harper: Ok, we're about halfway, any other big blockers?
[00:12:01] Jon Ruiz: Not blocker, just want to make sure legal and security are aligned. We'll loop them in once we see the SOC2 docs.
[00:12:08] Speaker 1: We'll need that and the DPA draft.
[00:12:11] Alex Harper: Noted. I'll send both.
[00:12:15] [00:12:15] Priya Singh: Final demo note: Console exposes a compatibility heatmap that overlays kernel maturity and quantization viability. You can export a shortlist CSV with the top 5 recommended variants per route. That CSV is what we usually attach to the bench report.
[00:12:30] Maya Patel: That'll be helpful to present to our internal stakeholders.
[00:12:34] Tom Reyes: After the bench we'll also include a routing recommendation — e.g., route clinical-short -> odysseus-13b on H100, admin-short -> luma-7b quant on T4, fallback to aurora-14b-opt if quality fails.
[00:12:49] [00:12:49] Jon Ruiz: Sounds good. Let's confirm next steps and owners.
[00:12:52] Alex Harper: I'll summarize: Alex to share security pack + catalog spreadsheet by 2026-10-09; Priya to provision a bench slot and runner and send instructions by 2026-10-13; LighthouseHealth sends prompt set and SLOs by 2026-10-11.
[00:13:06] Maya Patel: Agreed. Anything else?
[00:13:09] Sara Kim: No, that's it from product.
[00:13:11] Speaker 1: I'll be watching for the SOC2 and DPA.
[00:13:14] Alex Harper: Great. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the bench and a 2-hour working session for results review.
[00:13:22] [00:13:22] Jon Ruiz: Thanks everyone.
[00:13:24] Alex Harper: Thanks, talk soon.
[00:13:27] [END OF TRANSCRIPT]
